areas.label: Workloads & requirements
areas.question: What must the system achieve, for which workload, and how is success decided?

areas.label: Models & architectures
areas.question: What does the model compute, and how does its structure set system cost?

areas.label: Quantitative system models
areas.question: Which simple models predict where time, memory, and money go?

areas.label: Hardware & accelerators
areas.question: How do processors, memory, and chip-level power shape what ML workloads can achieve?

areas.label: Frameworks, compilers & runtimes
areas.question: How is a model program expressed, transformed, and executed efficiently on hardware?

areas.label: Parallelism & distributed execution
areas.question: How is one workload split across many devices, and what does coordination cost?

areas.label: Datacenter infrastructure & fleet
areas.question: How are AI datacenters built, connected, fed, and shared across many jobs?

areas.label: Data engineering
areas.question: How is data acquired, labeled, curated, validated, stored, and kept trustworthy?

areas.label: Training & adaptation
areas.question: How are models trained and adapted, and what does that demand from the system?

areas.label: Model evaluation & testing
areas.question: How do we know a model and the system around it behave well enough, and for whom?

areas.label: Deployment & serving
areas.question: How are trained models delivered to users within latency, throughput, and cost targets?

areas.label: MLOps & operations
areas.question: How is a deployed ML system versioned, observed, changed, and eventually retired?

areas.label: Performance, efficiency & benchmarking
areas.question: How do we measure, compare, and reduce the time, memory, and energy a workload consumes?

areas.label: Reliability & fault tolerance
areas.question: How does the system keep working, or fail safely, when components fail at scale?

areas.label: Security & privacy
areas.question: How do we protect ML systems and the data they touch from adversaries and leakage?

areas.label: Safety & assurance
areas.question: How do we argue, enforce, and verify that a system will not cause unacceptable harm?

areas.label: Responsible AI
areas.question: How do we ensure the system's outcomes are fair, accountable, transparent, and governed?

areas.label: Sustainability & cost
areas.question: What does the system cost in energy, carbon, water, and money over its lifetime?

areas.label: Agentic systems
areas.question: What does it take to engineer models that plan and act through tools over many steps?

areas.label: Embodied & physical systems
areas.question: What changes when ML closes the loop with sensors, actuators, and the physical world?

requirements-slos.label: Requirements, SLOs & baselines
requirements-slos.definition: Stating measurable targets for a system's behavior and service, and the baselines and budgets against which they are judged.

workload-characterization.label: Workload characterization
workload-characterization.definition: Describing a workload's compute, memory, data, and traffic demands, and where it runs, so it can be engineered and provisioned for.

objectives-decisions.label: Objectives, proxies & decision policies
objectives-decisions.definition: How learned outputs become decisions, how optimized proxies relate to intended outcomes, and how competing objectives are traded.

model-families.label: Model families
model-families.definition: The classical and neural model regimes, with their inductive assumptions, viewed as workloads with characteristic compute and memory profiles.

architecture-blocks.label: Architecture building blocks
architecture-blocks.definition: The layer-level operations from which neural models are composed and whose shapes determine compute, memory, and data movement.

conditional-computation.label: Sparse & conditional computation
conditional-computation.definition: Model designs in which the computation performed varies per input, such as mixture-of-experts routing and early exit.

efficient-sequence-models.label: Long-context & efficient sequence models
efficient-sequence-models.definition: Sequence architectures that change how cost scales with context length, co-designed with the memory and compute they demand.

model-artifacts.label: Model artifacts & formats
model-artifacts.definition: The weights, graphs, metadata, and interface contracts that make a trained model a portable, loadable, deployable artifact.

roofline-locality.label: Roofline, performance models & simulation
roofline-locality.definition: Bound-based reasoning about whether computation is limited by arithmetic or data movement, and how reuse changes that limit.

speedup-limits.label: Amdahl's law & scaling efficiency
speedup-limits.definition: Models of how much speedup added parallel or accelerated resources can deliver, given serial work and fixed or growing problem sizes.

queueing-models.label: Queueing & capacity models
queueing-models.definition: Models relating arrivals, service rates, utilization, and waiting, used to predict latency and capacity under load.

scaling-laws.label: Scaling laws & compute-optimal allocation
scaling-laws.definition: Empirical relationships among parameters, data, and compute and observed quality, used to allocate training budgets.

accelerator-architecture.label: Accelerator architecture
accelerator-architecture.definition: The organization of processors specialized for ML: execution units, threading, dataflow, and the throughput they provide.

memory-systems.label: Memory hierarchy & bandwidth
memory-systems.definition: The storage levels of an ML processor, from registers and SRAM to HBM, and the capacity and bandwidth limits they impose.

node-interconnect.label: Host-device & scale-up interconnect
node-interconnect.definition: Links that move data between hosts and accelerators and among accelerators within a node or rack-scale domain.

chip-power-thermal.label: Chip power & thermal limits
chip-power-thermal.definition: Electrical and thermal limits at the chip and board level, and the runtime controls that keep execution within them.

edge-embedded-hardware.label: Edge & embedded hardware
edge-embedded-hardware.definition: Hardware for on-device ML, from mobile SoCs to microcontrollers, where memory and energy per inference bind.

programming-models.label: ML frameworks & programming models
programming-models.definition: The abstractions with which ML programs are written: tensors, computation graphs, execution modes, and automatic differentiation.

tensor-operators.label: Tensor operators & memory layout
tensor-operators.definition: Implementations of core tensor operations, such as matrix multiply, convolution, and attention, and the layouts that govern their efficiency.

gpu-programming.label: Kernel & GPU programming model
gpu-programming.definition: How kernels are written for parallel accelerators: the thread hierarchy, memory access patterns, occupancy, asynchronous data movement, and programming the matrix units.

ml-compilers.label: ML compilers & kernel optimization
ml-compilers.definition: Transforming model programs through intermediate representations into optimized kernels for target hardware.

runtime-dispatch.label: Runtime execution & dispatch
runtime-dispatch.definition: How a runtime launches and orders device work and manages device memory during execution.

data-loading.label: Data loading & input pipelines
data-loading.definition: Delivering training and inference inputs to accelerators fast enough: host-side loading and preprocessing, prefetching, and sampling minibatches from large or irregular data such as graphs.

numerics.label: Numerical formats & precision
numerics.definition: Number formats used in ML computation and the techniques that keep training and inference accurate at reduced precision.

parallelism.label: Parallelism strategies
parallelism.definition: Ways of partitioning a model's computation and state across devices, and how those dimensions are combined.

parallelism-planning.label: Parallelization planning & placement
parallelism-planning.definition: Choosing and changing how a model is partitioned across devices: describing devices as a mesh, searching or propagating sharding decisions, placing experts and stages on heterogeneous hardware, and resharding at run time.

collectives.label: Collective communication
collectives.definition: Group communication primitives and algorithms used by parallel ML, their cost models, and techniques to reduce or hide their cost.

coordination.label: Coordination & consensus
coordination.definition: Mechanisms by which distributed components agree on authoritative control state and tolerate stale or failed participants.

federated-learning.label: Federated & decentralized learning
federated-learning.definition: Training across devices or organizations that keep their data local, coordinated through a shared model.

datacenter-facilities.label: Datacenter power, cooling & facilities
datacenter-facilities.definition: Engineering of the buildings that house ML fleets: power provisioning, cooling, density, and facility efficiency.

network-fabrics.label: Network fabrics
network-fabrics.definition: Datacenter networks that connect accelerator nodes: transports, topologies, flow and congestion control, and in-network compute.

storage-systems.label: Storage & data delivery
storage-systems.definition: Storage systems that hold training data, checkpoints, and artifacts at scale and deliver them to accelerators fast enough.

cluster-scheduling.label: Cluster scheduling & orchestration
cluster-scheduling.definition: Allocating a shared cluster's accelerators to jobs over time: placement, gang allocation, fairness, preemption, and elasticity.

capacity-provisioning.label: Capacity planning & multi-tenancy
capacity-provisioning.definition: Provisioning fleet capacity and sharing it among tenants through quotas, accelerator sharing, and interference control.

data-collection.label: Data collection & labeling
data-collection.definition: Obtaining observations and supervisory targets whose sampling, coverage, and label quality are known and fit the task.

data-curation.label: Data selection & curation
data-curation.definition: Choosing, filtering, deduplicating, mixing, augmenting, and synthesizing training examples to maximize learning value per unit of compute and labeling cost.

data-quality.label: Data validation & feature engineering
data-quality.definition: Checking that recorded data is fit for use and transforming it into model inputs whose semantics and availability match training and serving.

data-pipelines.label: Data pipelines & storage formats
data-pipelines.definition: Engineering ingestion, batch and stream transformation, event-time semantics, storage formats, and schemas for training and serving data.

data-lineage.label: Data contracts, versioning & lineage
data-lineage.definition: Specifying, versioning, and tracing the datasets a system consumes so that dependencies, provenance, and changes are explicit.

data-leakage-skew.label: Leakage & training-serving skew
data-leakage-skew.definition: Ensuring examples use only information available at prediction time and that training and serving compute features identically and equally fresh.

learning-paradigms.label: Learning paradigms
learning-paradigms.definition: The ways supervision, self-generated targets, interaction, and demonstration produce learning signals, each with distinct data and compute demands.

training-optimization.label: Optimization & training dynamics
training-optimization.definition: The objectives, update rules, schedules, and batch regimes that determine whether and how efficiently training converges.

training-memory.label: Training memory & state
training-memory.definition: Accounting for and reducing the parameters, gradients, optimizer state, and activations a training step must hold.

experiment-management.label: Hyperparameter search & experiment management
experiment-management.definition: Allocating a finite budget of training runs across configurations, and recording runs so their outcomes can be compared and reproduced.

fine-tuning.label: Adaptation: fine-tuning, prompting & transfer
fine-tuning.definition: Adapting a pretrained model to a new task or behavior, by continued training of all or part of its parameters or by prompting without parameter updates.

post-training.label: Preference & RL post-training
post-training.definition: Training pretrained models against preference, reward-model, or verifiable-reward signals, and the rollout, scoring, and weight-synchronization systems that loop requires.

continual-learning.label: Continual & online learning
continual-learning.definition: Updating deployed models incrementally from new or streaming data while retaining prior competence.

evaluation-protocols.label: Evaluation design & experiments
evaluation-protocols.definition: Constructing offline splits and online experiments whose comparisons support the conclusions drawn from them.

metrics-uncertainty.label: Metrics, calibration & uncertainty
metrics-uncertainty.definition: Specifying what is measured and quantifying how far estimates and predicted probabilities can be trusted.

robustness-slices.label: Sliced & robustness evaluation
robustness-slices.definition: Measuring behavior separately across populations and conditions, and under deliberate shift or perturbation, rather than only in aggregate.

generative-agent-eval.label: Evaluating generative & agentic systems
generative-agent-eval.definition: Assessing open-ended outputs and multi-step runs where no single reference answer exists, using graders, sampling-aware metrics, and contamination controls.

ml-testing.label: ML testing & debugging
ml-testing.definition: Testing data, models, pipelines, and their integration against stated expectations when exact expected outputs are often unknown.

serving-architecture.label: Serving architectures
serving-architecture.definition: The structure through which predictions are produced and delivered, from offline batch scoring to online and serverless model servers, multi-model and multi-adapter hosting, and streaming speech services.

compound-ai.label: Compound AI systems & model routing
compound-ai.definition: Composing several models, retrievers, and tools into one application, and routing, cascading, caching, and gating requests across models to meet quality and cost targets.

latency-goodput.label: Latency, throughput & goodput
latency-goodput.definition: Defining and meeting per-request latency and useful-throughput targets, including tail behavior and token-level latency for generative services.

request-scheduling.label: Batching, admission & autoscaling
request-scheduling.definition: Policies that group, admit, distribute, and provision for requests so a service meets its targets under varying load.

llm-inference.label: LLM & generative inference
llm-inference.definition: Mechanisms specific to generative inference: managing attention state, separating prompt processing from token generation, accelerating autoregressive decoding, and reducing iterative denoising cost.

structured-generation.label: Decoding, sampling & structured output
structured-generation.definition: Controlling how tokens are selected and constraining generated output to required syntax or schemas.

test-time-compute.label: Test-time compute
test-time-compute.definition: Spending additional inference computation on reasoning, sampling, search, and verification to raise output quality under a budget.

retrieval-rag.label: Retrieval & vector search
retrieval-rag.definition: Selecting relevant records from an external corpus by lexical, dense, or hybrid search and supplying them to a model at inference.

on-device-deployment.label: On-device & edge deployment
on-device-deployment.definition: Converting, packaging, executing, and updating models on phones, embedded devices, and microcontrollers under memory, energy, and connectivity limits.

release-management.label: Versioning, rollout & rollback
release-management.definition: Identifying, gating, and progressively exposing model releases, with the ability to return to a known-good configuration.

monitoring.label: Monitoring & observability
monitoring.definition: Instrumenting deployed systems and detecting, from logged signals, changes in inputs, outputs, quality, and health.

drift-retraining.label: Drift, feedback loops & retraining
drift-retraining.definition: Understanding how deployment data and outcomes change, including changes the system itself causes, and deciding when and how to update the model.

incident-response.label: Incident response
incident-response.definition: Detecting, triaging, mitigating, and learning from production failures, including attributing them to data, model, or infrastructure causes.

pipelines-reproducibility.label: ML pipelines & reproducibility
pipelines-reproducibility.definition: Automating the steps that produce models and controlling their environments and configuration so runs can be repeated.

ml-platforms.label: ML platforms, teams & technical debt
ml-platforms.definition: Shared internal platforms, team structures, and debt management that let an organization operate many models at sustainable cost.

retirement.label: Model retirement
retirement.definition: Ending a model's service by migrating its consumers, archiving what must be kept, and deleting data and resources that are no longer justified.

profiling-utilization.label: Profiling & utilization
profiling-utilization.definition: Measuring where execution time and resources go under a stated workload, and expressing how much of the hardware's capacity does useful model work.

system-benchmarking.label: System benchmarking
system-benchmarking.definition: Measuring training and inference system performance under specified workloads, quality targets, load scenarios, and run rules so results are comparable.

model-compression.label: Model compression
model-compression.definition: Techniques that shrink a trained or training model's parameters, precision, or rank to reduce memory, compute, and latency at a measured cost in quality.

hardware-aware-design.label: Hardware-aware model design
hardware-aware-design.definition: Choosing or searching model architectures against a target device's measured cost, so that quality and efficiency are optimized together rather than compressed after the fact.

failure-semantics.label: Failure models, retries & degradation
failure-semantics.definition: Declared failure assumptions and the service-level mechanisms (retries, idempotency, replication, circuit breaking, degradation) that keep requests correct and available when components fail.

checkpoint-recovery.label: Checkpointing & elastic recovery
checkpoint-recovery.definition: Persisting recoverable state for long-running jobs and choosing checkpoint frequency and recovery strategy to minimize lost work and restart cost under a given failure rate.

hardware-faults.label: Hardware faults & silent data corruption
hardware-faults.definition: How hardware fails in a fleet, from fail-stop crashes to gray and silent faults, how often it fails, and how such faults are detected and contained.

fault-injection.label: Fault injection & resilience testing
fault-injection.definition: Deliberately introducing software, infrastructure, or hardware faults under controlled scope to verify that detection, recovery, and degradation work as designed.

ml-attacks.label: Threat models & adversarial attacks
ml-attacks.definition: Specifying adversaries against learned systems and the attacks they mount on training data, model inputs, and instruction boundaries, with the defenses aimed at each.

model-supply-chain.label: Model & supply-chain security
model-supply-chain.definition: Protecting models as valuable artifacts from theft and tampering, and protecting the chain of datasets, pretrained weights, libraries, and builds that produce them.

privacy-dp.label: Privacy leakage & differential privacy
privacy-dp.definition: Privacy requirements for data about people, the attacks that extract it from models and outputs, and formal or architectural mechanisms that bound or remove that leakage.

access-isolation.label: Access control & isolation
access-isolation.definition: Constraining who may act, what code may reach, and which parties can observe data in use, through authorization, least privilege, isolation, and hardware-rooted trust.

hazards-operating-domain.label: Hazard analysis & operating domains
hazards-operating-domain.definition: Identifying how a system can contribute to harm, including hazards from functional insufficiency rather than faults, and fixing the operating conditions within which safety claims are made.

runtime-enforcement.label: Runtime assurance & safety filters
runtime-enforcement.definition: Mechanisms that monitor a learned component at run time and override, constrain, or replace its outputs so the system stays within a verified safe set.

verification-validation.label: Safety verification & validation
verification-validation.definition: Producing evidence that a system meets its safety requirements across its operating domain, through scenario testing, falsification, formal proof, and statistical validation of rare failures.

safety-cases.label: Safety cases, standards & certification
safety-cases.definition: Structured arguments that a system is acceptably safe for a defined use, the standards that set what evidence is required, and the field indicators that keep the argument valid after release.

fairness-bias.label: Fairness & bias
fairness-bias.definition: Specifying, measuring, and mitigating how a system's outcomes and errors differ across people and groups.

transparency-explainability.label: Explainability & documentation
transparency-explainability.definition: Making model behavior understandable to the people who build, deploy, and are affected by it, through explanations, interpretable models, and standardized documentation of models and data.

human-oversight.label: Human oversight & contestability
human-oversight.definition: Arrangements that let people supervise, intervene in, take over from, and challenge consequential system decisions, and the human-factors limits on doing so.

governance-regulation.label: AI governance, audit & regulation
governance-regulation.definition: Organizational and legal mechanisms that identify, assess, and control AI risk across a system's life, including risk-management frameworks, impact assessments, audits, and regulation.

energy-carbon.label: Energy & carbon accounting
energy-carbon.definition: Measuring the energy a workload consumes and converting it to operational emissions under declared boundaries, and scheduling work to reduce both.

embodied-lifecycle.label: Embodied carbon & lifecycle impact
embodied-lifecycle.definition: Environmental impacts beyond operating energy, from manufacturing emissions and water to hardware lifetime and disposal, assessed over the full hardware lifecycle.

cost-economics.label: Cost, TCO & unit economics
cost-economics.definition: Monetary accounting for ML systems, from total cost of ownership to cost per token or accepted outcome, and the architectural choices that lower cost at fixed quality.

context-memory.label: Context engineering & agent memory
context-memory.definition: Deciding what information enters each model call over a long task, and maintaining persistent memory the agent can write, consolidate, and retrieve across calls and sessions.

tool-interfaces.label: Tool use & action interfaces
tool-interfaces.definition: The interfaces through which a model acts on the world, including structured tool calls, tool discovery protocols, computer use, and the effects and authority those actions carry.

agent-harness.label: Agent harness & control loop
agent-harness.definition: The runtime that owns an agent's loop of model calls and tool actions, enforcing budgets, stopping rules, and approval gates and recording the trajectory.

durable-execution.label: Durable execution & agent state
durable-execution.definition: Persisting an agent's progress so long-running trajectories survive crashes, pauses, and redeployments without repeating completed effects, and can be replayed for debugging.

multi-agent.label: Multi-agent orchestration
multi-agent.definition: Decomposing a task across several model-driven agents and coordinating their delegation, shared state, and results, including when coordination costs outweigh the benefit.

perception-sensing.label: Sensing, perception & fusion
perception-sensing.definition: Turning time-stamped measurements from physical sensors into task-relevant estimates of the scene, including calibration, synchronization, and fusion across modalities.

state-estimation.label: State estimation, localization & mapping
state-estimation.definition: Inferring a robot's and its environment's latent state and uncertainty over time, through recursive filtering, localization and mapping, and learned predictive world models.

planning-control.label: Motion planning & control
planning-control.definition: Generating feasible, collision-free motions and closing feedback loops that drive a physical system along them under dynamics, contact, and actuation limits.

real-time-systems.label: Real-time & mixed-criticality computing
real-time-systems.definition: Guaranteeing that sensing, inference, and control complete within deadlines on shared embedded hardware, and isolating safety-critical functions from less trusted ones.

robot-learning.label: Robot learning & sim-to-real
robot-learning.definition: Learning robot policies from teleoperated demonstrations, simulation, and pretrained vision-language backbones, and transferring them to physical hardware.

mlsys.process-group-rendezvous.label: Distributed job launch and process groups
mlsys.process-group-rendezvous.subject: collectives
